name: Mount Gilboa
what: A mountain ridge at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley.
today: The Gilboa ridge in northern Israel.
key: Saul and his sons died on Mount Gilboa fighting the Philistines (1 Samuel 31).
David's lament asked that no dew or rain fall on Gilboa (2 Samuel 1).
Chronicles records Saul's death on Mount Gilboa (1 Chronicles 10).

name: Bezer
what: A city of refuge on the tableland east of the Jordan in the territory of Reuben.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly Umm el-Amad, near Madaba, Jordan.
key: Moses sets apart Bezer as a city of refuge for Reuben (Deuteronomy 4).
Bezer is confirmed as one of the six cities of refuge (Joshua 20).
Bezer is given to the Levites of the clan of Merari (Joshua 21).
Bezer is listed again among the Merarite Levitical cities (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Gilboa
what: A mountain ridge at the southeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley, where Saul died.
today: Mount Gilboa, in northern Israel near Beit She'an.
key: Saul gathered Israel at Gilboa, facing the Philistine army camped at Shunem (1 Samuel 28).
In his lament, David asked that no dew or rain fall on Gilboa (2 Samuel 1).
The Philistines had killed Saul on Gilboa, and David later reburied his bones (2 Samuel 21).

name: Taanach
what: A Canaanite city on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley, near Megiddo.
today: Tell Ta'annek, near Jenin in the northern West Bank.
key: Joshua defeated the king of Taanach (Joshua 12).
Manasseh received Taanach but did not drive out its Canaanites (Judges 1).
Taanach was given to the Levites of Kohath's clan (Joshua 21).
Deborah's song says the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach (Judges 5).
It belonged to one of Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kings 4).

name: Aner
what: A Levitical town in the western half-tribe of Manasseh, given to the Kohathite clans.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly the same as Taanach in northern Israel.
key: From the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner and Bileam went to the remaining Kohathite clans (1 Chronicles 6).
Joshua's parallel list names Taanach and Gath-rimmon from western Manasseh instead (Joshua 21).

name: Babylon
what: The capital of the Babylonian Empire on the Euphrates, where Judah was taken into exile.
today: Ruins near Hillah, Iraq
key: Hezekiah showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon (2 Kings 20).
Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and carried its king and people to Babylon (2 Kings 24).
Jeremiah wrote to the exiles, telling them to seek the welfare of Babylon (Jeremiah 29).
Daniel read the writing on the wall the night Babylon fell (Daniel 5).
John saw the fall of Babylon the great, the city opposed to God (Revelation 18).

name: Shinar
what: The ancient name for the plain of southern Mesopotamia, where Babylon stood.
today: Southern Iraq.
key: Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel and other cities in Shinar (Genesis 10).
People settled on a plain in Shinar and built the tower of Babel (Genesis 11).
Achan coveted and stole a beautiful cloak from Shinar (Joshua 7).
Nebuchadnezzar carried temple vessels to the land of Shinar (Daniel 1).
Zechariah saw wickedness carried in a basket to Shinar (Zechariah 5).

name: Mesopotamia
what: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, homeland of Abraham's family.
today: Mainly modern Iraq, with parts of Syria and Turkey.
key: Abraham's servant traveled to Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 24).
Balaam was hired from Pethor in Mesopotamia to curse Israel (Deuteronomy 23).
Othniel delivered Israel from Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia (Judges 3).
Jews and converts from Mesopotamia heard the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2).
Stephen recalled that God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia before Haran (Acts 7).

name: Babylonia
what: The land of Babylon in southern Mesopotamia, where Judah's exiles lived after Jerusalem fell.
today: Southern Iraq.
key: Sheshbazzar brought the temple vessels from Babylonia to Jerusalem (Ezra 1).
Darius found Cyrus's decree in the archives in Babylonia (Ezra 6).
Artaxerxes let Ezra take silver and gold gathered in Babylonia (Ezra 7).
Family heads went up with Ezra from Babylonia (Ezra 8).

name: Babel
what: An ancient city in the land of Shinar where people built a tower and God confused their language.
today: The ruins of Babylon, near Hillah, Iraq.
key: Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel and other cities in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10).
People settled in Shinar and began building a city and a tower to make a name for themselves (Genesis 11).
The Lord confused their language and scattered them over the face of all the earth (Genesis 11).

name: Dura
what: A plain in the province of Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar set up his golden image.
today: Exact site unknown; near Babylon, Iraq.
key: Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image ninety feet high on the plain of Dura (Daniel 3).
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to bow and were thrown into the furnace, but God delivered them (Daniel 3).

name: Harod
what: A spring near Mount Gilboa where Gideon camped; two of David's mighty men were called men of Harod.
today: Likely Ain Jalud at the foot of Mount Gilboa, northern Israel.
key: Gideon and his army camped beside the spring of Harod, with Midian's camp to the north (Judges 7).
There the LORD reduced Gideon's army, sending home the fearful and testing the rest at the water (Judges 7).
Shammah of Harod and Elika of Harod are listed among David's thirty mighty men (2 Samuel 23).

name: Jezreel
what: A town in Issachar overlooking the Jezreel Valley, a royal residence of King Ahab.
today: Tel Jezreel, near Afula, northern Israel
key: Elijah ran ahead of Ahab's chariot to Jezreel (1 Kings 18).
Jezebel had Naboth killed so Ahab could take his vineyard in Jezreel (1 Kings 21).
Jehu killed King Joram, and Jezebel was thrown from a window in Jezreel (2 Kings 9).
Hosea named his son Jezreel as a sign of judgment on Jehu's house (Hosea 1).

name: Valley of Jezreel
what: A broad, fertile valley in northern Israel, a frequent battlefield and route for armies.
today: The Jezreel Valley, in northern Israel between Galilee and Samaria.
key: Canaanites in the Valley of Jezreel had iron chariots, troubling the tribe of Joseph (Joshua 17).
Midianites and Amalekites crossed the Jordan and camped in the Valley of Jezreel against Gideon (Judges 6).
God says he will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel (Hosea 1).

name: Ramoth-gilead
what: A fortified city in Gilead east of the Jordan, often contested between Israel and Syria.
today: Likely Tell er-Rumeith, northern Jordan
key: Ramoth-gilead was the center of one of Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kings 4).
Ahab was killed by a random arrow fighting the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22).
King Joram was wounded fighting Hazael at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kings 8).
Elisha's servant anointed Jehu king of Israel at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kings 9).

name: Mizpah
what: A town in Gilead east of the Jordan, named for the watchpost set up by Jacob and Laban.
today: Exact site unknown; somewhere in Gilead, Jordan.
key: Jacob and Laban made a covenant heap called Mizpah as a witness between them (Genesis 31).
Israel camped at Mizpah to face the Ammonites (Judges 10).
Jephthah's daughter came out to meet him at his home in Mizpah (Judges 11).
Hosea rebuked Israel's leaders as a snare at Mizpah (Hosea 5).

name: Ramoth
what: A city in Gilead east of the Jordan, assigned to Gad as a city of refuge.
today: Likely Tell er-Rumeith, in northern Jordan near the Syrian border.
key: Moses set apart Ramoth in Gilead as a city of refuge for Gad (Deuteronomy 4).
Joshua confirmed Ramoth in Gilead among the cities of refuge (Joshua 20).
Ramoth in Gilead was given to the Merarite Levites from Gad's territory (Joshua 21).

name: Megiddo
what: A fortified city guarding a key pass into the Jezreel Valley.
today: Tel Megiddo in the Jezreel Valley, northern Israel.
key: Manasseh did not drive out the Canaanites of Megiddo (Judges 1).
Deborah's song recalls the kings of Canaan fighting by the waters of Megiddo (Judges 5).
Solomon rebuilt Megiddo with forced labor (1 Kings 9).
King Ahaziah of Judah fled from Jehu and died at Megiddo (2 Kings 9).
King Josiah was killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23).

name: Armageddon
what: The place where, in John's vision, the kings of the earth assemble for battle on the great day of God.
today: Commonly linked with Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley, northern Israel.
key: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east (Revelation 16).
Demonic spirits gather the kings of the whole world for battle on the great day of God (Revelation 16).
The kings are assembled at the place called in Hebrew Armageddon (Revelation 16).

name: Shunem
what: A town in the Jezreel Valley in Issachar, home of the Shunammite woman Elisha helped.
today: Modern Sulam, near Afula in northern Israel.
key: Shunem is listed among the towns of Issachar (Joshua 19).
The Philistines camped at Shunem before the battle in which Saul died (1 Samuel 28).
A woman of Shunem hosted Elisha, who later raised her son to life (2 Kings 4).

name: Ophrah
what: Gideon's hometown, belonging to the clan of Abiezer in Manasseh.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly near Afula in the Jezreel Valley, Israel.
key: The angel of the LORD called Gideon at Ophrah, where he built an altar (Judges 6).
Gideon made a gold ephod at Ophrah, which became a snare to Israel (Judges 8).
Gideon was buried at Ophrah (Judges 8).
Abimelech killed his seventy brothers on one stone at Ophrah (Judges 9).

name: Dor
what: A Canaanite port city on the Mediterranean coast south of Mount Carmel.
today: Tel Dor, on the coast south of Haifa, Israel.
key: The king of Dor is listed among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
Dor is given to Manasseh, but the Canaanites remain there (Joshua 17).
Manasseh fails to drive out the inhabitants of Dor (Judges 1).
Dor is listed among the towns held by the descendants of Joseph (1 Chronicles 7).

name: Edrei
what: A royal city of Og king of Bashan, east of the Jordan.
today: Daraa, in southern Syria near the Jordanian border.
key: Og king of Bashan came out to fight Israel at Edrei and was defeated (Numbers 21).
God told Moses not to fear Og, and Israel struck him down (Deuteronomy 3).
Og had reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei (Joshua 12).
Edrei was allotted to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13).

name: En-dor
what: A town south of Mount Tabor, best known as the home of the medium Saul consulted.
today: Likely near the village of Indur, south of Mount Tabor, Israel.
key: En-dor was assigned to Manasseh, though it lay within Issachar and Asher (Joshua 17).
On the eve of battle, a disguised Saul consulted a medium at En-dor (1 Samuel 28).
The psalmist recalls Sisera and Jabin, who perished at En-dor (Psalms 83).

name: Sharon
what: The fertile coastal plain of Israel between Joppa and Mount Carmel.
today: The Sharon Plain along Israel's central Mediterranean coast.
key: David's herds grazed in Sharon under Shitrai (1 Chronicles 27).
The bride calls herself a rose of Sharon (Song of Solomon 2).
Isaiah foretold that the splendor of Sharon would be given to the wilderness (Isaiah 35).
God promised Sharon would become a pasture for his people (Isaiah 65).
Residents of Lydda and Sharon turned to the Lord after Aeneas was healed (Acts 9).

name: East Manasseh
what: The territory east of the Jordan given to half the tribe of Manasseh, covering northern Gilead and Bashan.
today: Northern Jordan and southern Syria, including the Golan Heights area.
key: Moses gave Gilead and the former kingdom of Og to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32).
Jair son of Manasseh took the region of Argob and named its villages after himself (Deuteronomy 3).
Moses' allotment to the half-tribe stretched from Mahanaim through all Bashan (Joshua 13).
Because of their unfaithfulness, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser carried the half-tribe into exile (1 Chronicles 5).
Manasseh receives a portion in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land (Ezekiel 48).

name: Issachar
what: The tribal territory of Issachar, centered on the fertile Jezreel Valley in northern Israel.
today: The eastern Jezreel Valley and lower Galilee in northern Israel.
key: Manasseh held some towns within Issachar, such as Beth-shean (Joshua 17).
Issachar received the fourth lot, including Jezreel and Shunem (Joshua 19).
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah served as Solomon's district officer in Issachar (1 Kings 4).
Issachar receives a portion in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land (Ezekiel 48).

name: Lo-debar
what: A town in Gilead east of the Jordan, home of Machir son of Ammiel.
today: Exact site unknown; in Gilead in northern Jordan.
key: David found Mephibosheth living in Machir's house at Lo-debar and showed him kindness (2 Samuel 9).
Machir of Lo-debar brought food and supplies to David during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17).

name: Jokneam
what: A Canaanite town near Mount Carmel, later a Levitical city in Zebulun.
today: Tel Yoqneam, at the northwestern edge of the Jezreel Valley, Israel.
key: The king of Jokneam in Carmel was among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
Zebulun's border reached the brook east of Jokneam (Joshua 19).
Jokneam was given from Zebulun to the Merarite Levites (Joshua 21).

name: Tabor
what: A town in Zebulun near Mount Tabor, given to the Merarite Levites.
today: Exact site unknown; near Mount Tabor in northern Israel.
key: Zebulun's border ran by Chisloth-tabor, possibly the same town (Joshua 19).
Tabor and its pasturelands were given from Zebulun to the Merarite Levites (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Chisloth-tabor
what: A place on the border of Zebulun near Mount Tabor, on the way toward Daberath.
today: Possibly Iksal, near Nazareth in northern Israel.
key: Zebulun's boundary ran east from Sarid to the border of Chisloth-tabor (Joshua 19).
From there the boundary went on to Daberath and up to Japhia (Joshua 19).

name: Tabor
what: A rounded mountain rising from the Jezreel Valley in Lower Galilee.
today: Mount Tabor, in northern Israel.
key: Tabor marked the border of Issachar (Joshua 19).
Gideon asked Zebah and Zalmunna about the men they killed at Tabor (Judges 8).
The psalmist says Tabor and Hermon praise God's name (Psalms 89).
Hosea accused Israel's leaders of being a net spread on Tabor (Hosea 5).

name: Mount Tabor
what: A prominent rounded mountain at the northeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley.
today: Mount Tabor, east of Nazareth in northern Israel.
key: Deborah told Barak to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor (Judges 4).
Barak went down from Mount Tabor and the LORD routed Sisera's army (Judges 4).

name: Harosheth-hagoyim
what: The home base of Sisera, commander of the Canaanite king Jabin's army.
today: Exact site uncertain; probably near the Kishon River in northern Israel.
key: Sisera, commander of Jabin's army, lived in Harosheth-hagoyim (Judges 4).
Barak pursued Sisera's chariots and army all the way to Harosheth-hagoyim (Judges 4).

name: Daberath
what: A town near Mount Tabor on the border of Zebulun, later given to the Levites.
today: Likely Daburiyya, at the western foot of Mount Tabor, Israel.
key: Daberath is named on the boundary of Zebulun's territory (Joshua 19).
Daberath was given from Issachar's land to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 21).
The Chronicler lists Daberath again among the Levites' towns (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Galilee
what: The northern region of Israel around the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus grew up and did most of his ministry.
today: Northern Israel
key: Kedesh in Galilee was set apart as a city of refuge (Joshua 20).
Isaiah foretold a great light for Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9).
Jesus began preaching and calling disciples in Galilee (Matthew 4).
At a wedding in Cana in Galilee, Jesus turned water into wine (John 2).
The risen Jesus met the eleven on a mountain in Galilee and sent them out (Matthew 28).

name: Nazareth
what: A small town in Galilee where Jesus was raised.
today: Nazareth, northern Israel
key: The angel Gabriel announced Jesus' birth to Mary in Nazareth (Luke 1).
Joseph settled the family in Nazareth after returning from Egypt (Matthew 2).
Jesus was rejected in the synagogue of his hometown, Nazareth (Luke 4).
Nathanael asked if anything good could come out of Nazareth (John 1).
Peter healed a lame man in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth (Acts 3).

name: Zebulun
what: The tribal territory of Zebulun in lower Galilee, between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean.
today: Lower Galilee, northern Israel
key: Jacob said Zebulun would dwell at the shore of the sea (Genesis 49).
Joshua assigned Zebulun its inheritance in Galilee (Joshua 19).
Isaiah foresaw honor coming to the land of Zebulun and Naphtali (Isaiah 9).
Jesus' ministry in Capernaum fulfilled Isaiah's word about Zebulun (Matthew 4).

name: Mount Carmel
what: A wooded mountain ridge on Israel's northern coast, overlooking the Jezreel Valley.
today: The Carmel ridge near Haifa, Israel.
key: Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel when God sent fire (1 Kings 18).
Elisha went to Mount Carmel after leaving Bethel (2 Kings 2).
The Shunammite woman found Elisha at Mount Carmel after her son died (2 Kings 4).

name: Cana
what: A village in Galilee where Jesus performed his first sign, turning water into wine.
today: Likely Khirbet Qana, north of Nazareth, Israel.
key: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding, his first sign (John 2).
At Cana Jesus heals an official's son who lies sick in Capernaum (John 4).
Nathanael of Cana is among the disciples who meet the risen Jesus (John 21).

name: Kanah
what: A town on the northern border of Asher's inheritance, toward Sidon.
today: Likely Qana, southeast of Tyre in southern Lebanon
key: Kanah is listed with Ebron, Rehob, and Hammon on the boundary of Asher (Joshua 19).
From these towns Asher's border reached as far as Sidon the Great (Joshua 19).

name: Kishon
what: A river flowing through the Jezreel Valley to the Mediterranean near Mount Carmel.
today: The Kishon River (Nahal Kishon), in northern Israel.
key: Sisera gathered his chariots at the Kishon to fight Barak (Judges 4).
Deborah's song says the torrent Kishon swept the enemy away (Judges 5).
Elijah executed the prophets of Baal at the brook Kishon (1 Kings 18).
The psalmist asks God to deal with enemies as with Sisera at the Kishon (Psalms 83).

name: Aphek
what: A town east of the Sea of Galilee where Israel defeated the Syrians.
today: Likely near Afik, east of the Sea of Galilee, Golan Heights.
key: Ben-hadad attacks at Aphek, Israel defeats Syria, and a wall falls on survivors (1 Kings 20).
Elisha's arrow of victory promises that Joash will defeat the Syrians in Aphek (2 Kings 13).

name: Tiberias
what: A city on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, which gave the lake one of its names.
today: Tiberias, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, Israel.
key: John names the lake as the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias (John 6).
After Jesus fed the five thousand, boats from Tiberias came near the place where the crowd had eaten (John 6).

name: Bashan
what: A fertile highland east of the Sea of Galilee, known for its cattle and oaks.
today: Golan Heights and southern Syria
key: Israel defeated Og king of Bashan at Edrei (Numbers 21).
Moses gave Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 3).
The psalmist describes his enemies as strong bulls of Bashan (Psalms 22).
Amos rebuked the women of Samaria as cows of Bashan (Amos 4).

name: Golan
what: A city of refuge in Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, in the territory of Manasseh.
today: Possibly Sahem el-Jolan, southern Syria; it gave its name to the Golan Heights.
key: Moses sets apart Golan in Bashan as a city of refuge for Manasseh (Deuteronomy 4).
Golan is confirmed as one of the six cities of refuge (Joshua 20).
Golan is given to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 21).
Golan is listed again among the Gershonite Levitical cities (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Rephaim
what: An early people known for great stature, whose last king, Og, ruled Bashan east of the Jordan.
today: No single site; their land included Bashan, in northern Jordan and southern Syria.
key: The LORD promised Abraham's offspring the land of the Rephaim among other peoples (Genesis 15).
The Emim and Zamzummim, counted as Rephaim, were displaced by Moab and Ammon (Deuteronomy 2).
Og king of Bashan alone remained of the Rephaim; his iron bed was nine cubits long (Deuteronomy 3).
All Bashan, the region of Argob, was called the land of Rephaim (Deuteronomy 3).

name: Sea of Galilee
what: A freshwater lake in northern Israel, center of much of Jesus' ministry.
today: Lake Kinneret, in northern Israel.
key: Jesus called Peter and Andrew by the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4).
Jesus healed many by the Sea of Galilee and fed four thousand (Matthew 15).
Jesus healed a deaf man in the region by the Sea of Galilee (Mark 7).
Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee and fed five thousand (John 6).

name: Sea of Tiberias
what: Another name for the Sea of Galilee, taken from the city of Tiberias on its western shore.
today: Lake Kinneret (the Sea of Galilee), northern Israel.
key: Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias, and fed five thousand (John 6).
The risen Jesus appeared by the Sea of Tiberias and gave the disciples a great catch (John 21).
After breakfast on the shore, Jesus three times asked Peter whether he loved him (John 21).

name: Cyrene
what: A Greek city on the coast of North Africa with a large Jewish community.
today: Ruins at Shahhat, in eastern Libya.
key: Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry Jesus' cross (Matthew 27).
Mark names Simon of Cyrene as the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15).
Visitors from the parts of Libya near Cyrene heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2).
Men of Cyprus and Cyrene preached the Lord Jesus to Greeks at Antioch (Acts 11).
Lucius of Cyrene was a prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch (Acts 13).

name: Put
what: An African nation west of Egypt whose soldiers fought as Egypt's allies.
today: Likely Libya, west of Egypt.
key: Men of Put carrying shields marched in Egypt's army against Babylon (Jeremiah 46).
Ezekiel foretells that Put will fall by the sword along with Egypt (Ezekiel 30).
Nahum names Put among the helpers of Thebes, which still fell (Nahum 3).

name: Libya
what: The North African region west of Egypt, including the area around Cyrene.
today: Eastern Libya (Cyrenaica), North Africa.
key: Ezekiel listed Libya among Egypt's allies who would fall by the sword (Ezekiel 30).
Visitors from the parts of Libya near Cyrene heard the gospel in their own language at Pentecost (Acts 2).

name: Ashtaroth
what: A royal city of Bashan east of the Sea of Galilee, home of King Og.
today: Tell Ashtara, in southern Syria.
key: Og king of Bashan lived at Ashtaroth when Israel defeated him (Deuteronomy 1).
The Gibeonites cited Israel's victory over Og at Ashtaroth (Joshua 9).
Ashtaroth was allotted to the half-tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13).
It was given to the Levites of Gershon's clan (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Gennesaret
what: A fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, which also lent the lake its name.
today: The plain of Ginosar, on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, Israel.
key: After crossing the lake, Jesus landed at Gennesaret, and all who touched his garment were healed (Matthew 14).
Mark records people bringing the sick on mats as soon as Jesus reached Gennesaret (Mark 6).
By the lake of Gennesaret, Jesus taught from Peter's boat and called him after a great catch (Luke 5).

name: Capernaum
what: A fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus' base of ministry.
today: Ruins on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, Israel
key: Jesus left Nazareth and made his home in Capernaum (Matthew 4).
Jesus healed a centurion's servant at Capernaum (Matthew 8).
Jesus healed a paralyzed man lowered through a roof in Capernaum (Mark 2).
Jesus warned Capernaum for not repenting despite his mighty works (Matthew 11).
Jesus taught that he is the bread of life in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6).

name: Bethsaida
what: A fishing town near the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.
today: Likely et-Tell or el-Araj, near the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.
key: Philip, Andrew, and Peter were from Bethsaida (John 1).
Jesus fed the five thousand near Bethsaida (Luke 9).
Jesus healed a blind man at Bethsaida in two stages (Mark 8).
Jesus pronounced woe on Bethsaida for not repenting despite his mighty works (Matthew 11).
Greeks wishing to see Jesus approached Philip of Bethsaida (John 12).

name: Chorazin
what: A Galilean town near Capernaum that saw Jesus' mighty works but did not repent.
today: Korazim (Khirbet Karazeh), north of the Sea of Galilee, Israel.
key: Jesus pronounced woe on Chorazin and Bethsaida for not repenting despite his mighty works (Matthew 11).
He said Tyre and Sidon would have repented long ago had they seen such works (Matthew 11).
Jesus repeated the warning to Chorazin when sending out the seventy-two (Luke 10).

name: Asher
what: The tribal territory of Asher along the Mediterranean coast in northern Israel.
today: Coastal Galilee, northern Israel, into southern Lebanon
key: Moses blessed Asher with plenty and favor among his brothers (Deuteronomy 33).
Joshua assigned the coastal lands of the north to Asher (Joshua 19).
Asher failed to drive out the people of Acco and Sidon (Judges 1).
Asher stayed by the coast rather than join Deborah's battle (Judges 5).

name: Acco
what: A Mediterranean port city north of Mount Carmel, in the territory assigned to Asher.
today: Acre (Akko), on the coast of northern Israel.
key: Asher failed to drive out the inhabitants of Acco and Sidon (Judges 1).
Sailing from Tyre, Paul landed at Ptolemais and stayed a day with the believers there (Acts 21).

name: Achshaph
what: A Canaanite royal city in northern Canaan, later on the border of Asher.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly Tell Keisan, near Acco, Israel.
key: Jabin king of Hazor summons the king of Achshaph to fight Israel (Joshua 11).
The king of Achshaph is listed among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
Achshaph lies on the boundary of Asher's territory (Joshua 19).

name: Rehob
what: A town in the territory of Asher, later given to the Levites.
today: Exact site uncertain; in western Galilee near Acco, Israel.
key: Rehob is listed within the territory of Asher (Joshua 19).
Rehob is given to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 21).
Asher fails to drive out the inhabitants of Rehob (Judges 1).
Rehob is listed again among the Levitical cities (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Geshur
what: A small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee.
today: The Golan Heights region, east of the Sea of Galilee.
key: Israel did not drive out the Geshurites (Joshua 13).
David married Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, the mother of Absalom (2 Samuel 3).
Absalom fled to Geshur for three years after killing Amnon (2 Samuel 13).
Joab brought Absalom back from Geshur to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14).

name: Hazor
what: A major Canaanite city north of the Sea of Galilee.
today: Tel Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee in Israel.
key: Jabin king of Hazor led a northern coalition, and Joshua burned the city (Joshua 11).
Later, Jabin king of Canaan reigned in Hazor and oppressed Israel through Sisera (Judges 4).
Samuel recalled how God sold Israel into the hand of Sisera of Hazor (1 Samuel 12).
Solomon rebuilt Hazor with forced labor (1 Kings 9).
The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured Hazor and exiled its people (2 Kings 15).

name: Tishbe
what: The hometown of the prophet Elijah, who is called the Tishbite.
today: Exact site unknown; traditionally in Gilead, northern Jordan.
key: Elijah the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, announced a drought to King Ahab (1 Kings 17).
God sent Elijah the Tishbite to confront Ahab over Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21).
King Ahaziah recognized from a description that the prophet was Elijah the Tishbite (2 Kings 1).

name: Naphtali
what: The tribal territory of Naphtali in Galilee, west and north of the Sea of Galilee.
today: Eastern Galilee, northern Israel
key: Moses viewed all Naphtali from Mount Nebo before he died (Deuteronomy 34).
Kedesh in Naphtali was set apart as a city of refuge (Joshua 20).
Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured Naphtali and carried its people away (2 Kings 15).
Jesus settled in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah's word about Naphtali (Matthew 4).

name: Merom
what: Waters in upper Galilee where Joshua defeated the northern Canaanite kings led by Jabin of Hazor.
today: Exact site uncertain; likely springs in upper Galilee, northern Israel.
key: Jabin of Hazor and his allies camped together at the waters of Merom to fight Israel (Joshua 11).
Joshua attacked them suddenly at Merom, and the Lord gave them into Israel's hand (Joshua 11).
Israel hamstrung the enemy's horses and burned their chariots as the Lord had commanded (Joshua 11).

name: Accad
what: One of the first cities of Nimrod's kingdom, in the land of Shinar in southern Mesopotamia.
today: Akkad, in central Iraq; exact site unknown.
key: Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10).
From there he went into Assyria and built Nineveh and other cities (Genesis 10).

name: Kedesh
what: A fortified city of Naphtali in Upper Galilee and a city of refuge.
today: Tel Kedesh, northwest of Lake Hula in northern Israel.
key: Kedesh was allotted to Naphtali (Joshua 19).
Kedesh in Galilee was set apart as a city of refuge (Joshua 20).
Barak came from Kedesh, and Deborah went there with him to gather troops (Judges 4).
Tiglath-pileser captured Kedesh and exiled its people to Assyria (2 Kings 15).

name: Rehob
what: A town on the northern border of Asher's territory, listed toward Sidon.
today: Exact site unknown; in upper Galilee or southern Lebanon.
key: Rehob is listed on Asher's border with Hammon and Kanah, as far as Sidon (Joshua 19).
A second Rehob in Asher appears a few verses later near Aphek (Joshua 19).

name: Hammon
what: A town on the border of Asher's inheritance in the far north, toward Sidon.
today: Possibly Umm el-Amed, near the coast of southern Lebanon
key: Hammon is listed with Ebron, Rehob, and Kanah on the boundary of Asher (Joshua 19).
From these towns Asher's border reached as far as Sidon the Great (Joshua 19).

name: Argob
what: A region of Bashan with sixty fortified cities, taken from Og king of Bashan.
today: In Bashan, southern Syria; exact extent uncertain.
key: Israel captures the sixty cities of Argob from Og king of Bashan (Deuteronomy 3).
Jair of Manasseh takes the region of Argob and names it after himself (Deuteronomy 3).
Argob falls within the district of Solomon's officer Ben-geber (1 Kings 4).

name: Chebar
what: A canal in Babylonia where Jewish exiles lived and Ezekiel received visions.
today: Exact site unknown; likely a canal near Nippur in southern Iraq.
key: Among the exiles by the Chebar canal, Ezekiel saw visions of God (Ezekiel 1).
Ezekiel came to the exiles at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 3).
Ezekiel recognized the cherubim as the creatures he saw by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 10).
God's glory returning to the temple looked like the vision by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 43).

name: Maacah
what: A small Aramean kingdom north of Bashan, near the slopes of Mount Hermon.
today: Around the northern Golan Heights and southern Lebanon.
key: The Ammonites hire the king of Maacah and his men to fight David (2 Samuel 10).
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai of Maacah is among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23).
Chronicles records the king of Maacah and his troops joining the Ammonites (1 Chronicles 19).

name: Rehob
what: An Aramean town and district in the far north of Israel, near Dan and Lebo-hamath.
today: Exact site unknown; near Dan in far northern Israel or southern Lebanon.
key: The spies explored the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath (Numbers 13).
Laish, later Dan, lay in the valley belonging to Beth-rehob (Judges 18).
The Ammonites hired Syrians of Beth-rehob and Zobah to fight against David (2 Samuel 10).

name: Great Sea
what: The Mediterranean Sea, forming the western border of the Promised Land.
today: The Mediterranean Sea.
key: God set the Great Sea as the western boundary of Canaan (Numbers 34).
God promised Joshua land stretching to the Great Sea toward the sunset (Joshua 1).
Kings along the coast of the Great Sea gathered to fight Israel (Joshua 9).
In Ezekiel's vision, the river from the temple makes the Dead Sea teem with fish like the Great Sea (Ezekiel 47).

name: Caesarea Philippi
what: A Roman city at the foot of Mount Hermon, near the sources of the Jordan River.
today: Banias, at the foot of Mount Hermon in the Golan Heights.
key: Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked who people said he was, and Peter confessed him as the Christ (Matthew 16).
From then on Jesus began to show that he must suffer, be killed, and be raised (Matthew 16).
Mark records Peter's confession on the way to the villages of Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8).

name: Dan
what: A city at Israel's northern edge, formerly Laish, captured and renamed by the tribe of Dan.
today: Tel Dan, northern Israel
key: Abram pursued the kings who captured Lot as far as Dan (Genesis 14).
The Danites captured Laish, renamed it Dan, and set up a carved image (Judges 18).
All Israel from Dan to Beersheba recognized Samuel as a prophet (1 Samuel 3).
Jeroboam placed a golden calf at Dan (1 Kings 12).
Ben-hadad of Syria conquered Dan at King Asa's request (1 Kings 15).

name: Laish
what: A quiet, isolated city in the far north captured by the tribe of Dan and renamed Dan.
today: Tel Dan, in northern Israel.
key: Danite spies find the people of Laish quiet, unsuspecting, and far from help (Judges 18).
The Danites strike Laish and burn it (Judges 18).
The Danites rebuild the city and rename Laish as Dan (Judges 18).

name: Leshem
what: A city in the far north captured by the tribe of Dan and renamed Dan.
today: Tel Dan, in northern Israel.
key: When their territory proved too small, the Danites captured Leshem and renamed it Dan (Joshua 19).
Judges tells the fuller story, calling the city Laish and describing its capture and renaming (Judges 18).

name: Abel
what: A fortified town in the far north of Israel where the rebel Sheba took refuge.
today: Tel Abel Beth Maacah, near Metula, northern Israel.
key: Sheba son of Bichri flees to Abel, and Joab besieges the city (2 Samuel 20).
A wise woman of Abel persuades the city to throw Sheba's head to Joab, saving it (2 Samuel 20).

name: Abel-beth-maacah
what: A fortified town in the far north of Israel, near Dan, repeatedly struck by invading armies.
today: Tel Abel Beth Maacah, near Metula, northern Israel.
key: Joab besieged the rebel Sheba in Abel of Beth-maacah until a wise woman had his head thrown out (2 Samuel 20).
Ben-hadad of Syria attacked Israelite cities including Ijon, Dan, and Abel-beth-maacah (1 Kings 15).
Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured Abel-beth-maacah and carried its people into exile (2 Kings 15).

name: Beth-maacah
what: The district of a far-northern town, Abel of Beth-maacah, where the rebel Sheba took refuge from Joab.
today: Tel Abel Beth Maacah, near Metula, northern Israel.
key: Sheba son of Bichri passed through all the tribes and reached Abel of Beth-maacah (2 Samuel 20).
Joab besieged the city and built a siege mound against its wall (2 Samuel 20).
A wise woman persuaded the city to throw Sheba's head to Joab, and the siege ended (2 Samuel 20).

name: Tyre
what: A wealthy Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel.
today: Tyre (Sur), southern Lebanon
key: Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar and craftsmen to build David's house (2 Samuel 5).
Hiram supplied timber for Solomon's temple in exchange for food (1 Kings 5).
Ezekiel prophesied that Tyre would become a bare rock for drying nets (Ezekiel 26).
Jesus healed the daughter of a Gentile woman in the region of Tyre (Mark 7).
Paul stayed seven days with disciples at Tyre (Acts 21).

name: Ijon
what: A town in the far north of Israel, repeatedly taken by invading armies.
today: Likely Tell ed-Dibbin, in the Marjayoun valley of southern Lebanon.
key: At King Asa's request, Ben-hadad of Syria conquered Ijon (1 Kings 15).
Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured Ijon and deported its people (2 Kings 15).
The Chronicler repeats Ben-hadad's attack on Ijon (2 Chronicles 16).

name: Hermon
what: The tallest mountain in the region, marking the northern limit of Israel's conquest.
today: Mount Hermon, on the border of Lebanon and Syria, above the Golan Heights.
key: Israel took the land east of the Jordan as far as Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3).
Joshua's conquest reached Baal-gad below Mount Hermon (Joshua 11).
The psalmist remembers God from the land of Jordan and Hermon (Psalm 42).
Brothers dwelling in unity are like the dew of Hermon (Psalm 133).
The bride is called to come from the peaks of Senir and Hermon (Song of Solomon 4).

name: Mount Hermon
what: The highest mountain in the region, marking the northern limit of Israel's conquests east of the Jordan.
today: Mount Hermon, on the border of Syria and Lebanon above the Golan Heights.
key: Moses noted that Sidonians called Hermon Sirion and Amorites called it Senir (Deuteronomy 3).
Joshua's conquest reached the valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon (Joshua 11).
Og king of Bashan had ruled as far as Mount Hermon (Joshua 12).
The half-tribe of Manasseh settled from Bashan to Mount Hermon (1 Chronicles 5).

name: Senir
what: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon or part of its range.
today: Mount Hermon, on the Lebanon-Syria border.
key: Moses notes that the Amorites call Mount Hermon Senir (Deuteronomy 3).
The half-tribe of Manasseh settles from Bashan to Senir and Mount Hermon (1 Chronicles 5).
The bride is called to come down from the peaks of Senir and Hermon (Song of Solomon 4).
Tyre's ship planks are made of fir trees from Senir (Ezekiel 27).

name: Baal-gad
what: A town in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon, marking the northern limit of Joshua's conquest.
today: Exact site unknown; likely in southern Lebanon near the foot of Mount Hermon.
key: Joshua's conquest reached from Mount Halak in the south to Baal-gad in the north (Joshua 11).
Baal-gad is named again as the northern edge of the land Joshua took (Joshua 12).
God lists the region from Baal-gad toward Lebanon as land still to be possessed (Joshua 13).

name: Sirion
what: The Sidonian name for Mount Hermon, the highest mountain on Israel's northern border.
today: Mount Hermon, on the border of Lebanon, Syria, and the Golan Heights.
key: Moses notes that the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion (Deuteronomy 3).
The psalmist says the LORD's voice makes Sirion leap like a young wild ox (Psalms 29).
Jeremiah asks whether the snow ever leaves the crags of Sirion, contrasting Israel's unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 18).

name: Valley of Lebanon
what: The broad valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, below Mount Hermon.
today: The Beqaa Valley, Lebanon.
key: Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon marked the northern limit of Joshua's conquest (Joshua 11).
The valley is named again in the summary of kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).

name: Zarephath
what: A Phoenician town near Sidon where Elijah stayed with a widow during the drought.
today: Sarafand, on the coast of southern Lebanon between Tyre and Sidon.
key: God sends Elijah to a widow in Zarephath, whose flour and oil do not run out (1 Kings 17).
Elijah raises the widow's son to life (1 Kings 17).
Obadiah foresees Israelite exiles possessing the land as far as Zarephath (Obadiah 1).
Jesus notes Elijah was sent only to a widow of Zarephath in Sidon (Luke 4).

name: Syria
what: The Aramean kingdom north of Israel centered on Damascus; later a Roman province including Antioch.
today: Modern Syria
key: Ahab was killed in battle against the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22).
Naaman, commander of Syria's army, came to Elisha to be healed (2 Kings 5).
Syria and Israel joined against Ahaz, and Isaiah gave the Immanuel sign (Isaiah 7).
Quirinius was governor of Syria at the time of Jesus' birth (Luke 2).
After his conversion, Paul went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1).

name: Decapolis
what: A region of ten Greek-influenced cities, mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee.
today: Parts of northern Jordan, southern Syria, and northern Israel.
key: Great crowds from the Decapolis followed Jesus early in his ministry (Matthew 4).
The man freed from many demons proclaimed in the Decapolis what Jesus had done (Mark 5).
Jesus passed through the Decapolis region and healed a deaf man with a speech impediment (Mark 7).

name: Hadrach
what: A region in Syria named first in Zechariah's oracle of judgment on Israel's northern neighbors.
today: Likely the region of Hatarikka, near Hama, Syria.
key: The word of the Lord is against the land of Hadrach, and Damascus is its resting place (Zechariah 9).
The oracle continues with judgment on Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistine cities (Zechariah 9).
Zion's king then comes, humble and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9).

name: Damascus
what: An ancient city northeast of Israel, the capital of Syria (Aram).
today: Damascus, Syria
key: Abram pursued the captors of Lot as far as north of Damascus (Genesis 14).
Naaman boasted that the rivers of Damascus were better than the Jordan (2 Kings 5).
King Ahaz copied an altar he saw in Damascus for the temple (2 Kings 16).
Saul met the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9).
Paul escaped Damascus by being lowered over the wall in a basket (2 Corinthians 11).

name: Sidon
what: An ancient Phoenician port city north of Tyre on the Mediterranean coast.
today: Sidon (Saida), Lebanon
key: Israel served the gods of Sidon and other nations (Judges 10).
Elijah was sent to a widow in Zarephath, a town belonging to Sidon (1 Kings 17).
Ezekiel prophesied judgment against Sidon (Ezekiel 28).
Jesus passed through Sidon on his way back to the Sea of Galilee (Mark 7).
On the voyage to Rome, Paul was allowed to visit friends at Sidon (Acts 27).

name: Philistia
what: The coastal land of the Philistines in southwestern Canaan, with five major cities.
today: The southern coastal plain of Israel and the Gaza Strip.
key: Moses sang that terror gripped the inhabitants of Philistia (Exodus 15).
God declares that he shouts in triumph over Philistia (Psalms 60).
Philistia is named among nations counted as born in Zion (Psalms 87).
Isaiah warned Philistia not to rejoice at its oppressor's fall (Isaiah 14).

name: Phoenicia
what: The coastal region north of Israel that included the cities of Tyre and Sidon.
today: The coast of modern Lebanon and parts of northern Israel and Syria.
key: Believers scattered after Stephen's death traveled as far as Phoenicia, preaching to Jews (Acts 11).
Passing through Phoenicia, Paul and Barnabas reported the Gentiles' conversion, bringing great joy (Acts 15).
Paul boarded a ship crossing to Phoenicia on his way to Jerusalem (Acts 21).

name: Ahava
what: A river or canal in Babylonia where Ezra gathered the returning exiles before traveling to Jerusalem.
today: Exact site unknown; in Babylonia, modern Iraq.
key: Ezra gathers the exiles by the river that runs to Ahava and finds no Levites (Ezra 8).
Ezra proclaims a fast at the river Ahava to seek a safe journey from God (Ezra 8).
The company departs from the river Ahava, and God protects them on the way (Ezra 8).

name: Lebanon
what: The mountain range north of Israel, famous for its cedar forests.
today: Lebanon mountains, modern Lebanon
key: God promised Israel territory from the wilderness to Lebanon (Joshua 1).
Hiram of Tyre supplied cedars of Lebanon for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5).
Cedars from Lebanon were brought for rebuilding the temple after the exile (Ezra 3).
The righteous are said to grow like a cedar in Lebanon (Psalms 92).

name: Sepharvaim
what: A city conquered by Assyria, whose people were resettled in Samaria.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly in Syria or Mesopotamia.
key: Assyria resettled people from Sepharvaim in Samaria, where they burned their children to their gods (2 Kings 17).
The Assyrian commander asked where the gods of Sepharvaim were (2 Kings 18).
Sennacherib's letter boasted of the fallen king of Sepharvaim (2 Kings 19).
Isaiah records the same Assyrian taunts against Hezekiah (Isaiah 37).

name: Aphek
what: A town in the territory of Asher whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out.
today: Likely Tel Afek (Tell Kurdaneh), southeast of Acco in northern Israel.
key: Aphek is listed among the towns of Asher's inheritance, with Ummah and Rehob (Joshua 19).
Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Aphik, so the Canaanites lived among them (Judges 1).

name: Gebal
what: An ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, north of Sidon.
today: Byblos (Jbeil), on the coast of Lebanon north of Beirut.
key: Men of Gebal helped prepare timber and stone for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5).
Gebal is named among the nations conspiring against God's people (Psalms 83).
Gebal's skilled elders repaired the seams of Tyre's ships (Ezekiel 27).

name: Hazar-enan
what: A town marking the northeastern corner of the boundary of the promised land.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly in central Syria.
key: The Lord sets Hazar-enan as the end of Israel's northern boundary (Numbers 34).
Ezekiel names Hazar-enan on the northern boundary of the restored land (Ezekiel 47).
Ezekiel again names Hazar-enan at the northern limit of Dan's portion (Ezekiel 48).

name: Zobah
what: An Aramean kingdom north of Damascus.
today: Likely the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon and neighboring parts of Syria.
key: Saul fought against the kings of Zobah (1 Samuel 14).
David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah near the Euphrates (2 Samuel 8).
The Ammonites hired Syrians of Zobah to fight David, but Joab routed them (2 Samuel 10).
Igal of Zobah was among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23).
Rezon fled from Hadadezer of Zobah and became Solomon's adversary in Damascus (1 Kings 11).

name: Rimmon
what: A town in the far south of Judah, later allotted to Simeon.
today: Possibly Khirbet Umm er-Ramamin, north of Beersheba, Israel.
key: Rimmon is listed among the southernmost towns of Judah (Joshua 15).
Rimmon is allotted to the tribe of Simeon (Joshua 19).
Rimmon appears among the towns where Simeon's descendants lived (1 Chronicles 4).
Zechariah foresees the land leveled from Geba to Rimmon, south of Jerusalem (Zechariah 14).

name: Riblah
what: A town in Syria used as a military headquarters by Egyptian and Babylonian kings.
today: Ribleh, on the Orontes River south of Homs, Syria.
key: Pharaoh Neco imprisoned King Jehoahaz of Judah at Riblah (2 Kings 23).
At Riblah, Nebuchadnezzar killed Zedekiah's sons before his eyes and blinded him (2 Kings 25).
Nebuchadnezzar also executed the nobles of Judah at Riblah (Jeremiah 39).
Judah's chief priest and officials were executed at Riblah (Jeremiah 52).

name: Hena
what: A city conquered by Assyria, cited by Sennacherib's officials as proof that no god could resist them.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly along the middle Euphrates.
key: The Rabshakeh asked where the gods of Hena were, to shake Jerusalem's trust in God (2 Kings 18).
Sennacherib's letter to Hezekiah again asked what became of the king of Hena (2 Kings 19).
Isaiah records the same boast about Hena, before God delivered Jerusalem (Isaiah 37).

name: Ivvah
what: A city conquered by Assyria, cited by Sennacherib's officials as proof of their power.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly in Syria or Mesopotamia.
key: The Rabshakeh asked where the gods of Ivvah were, to frighten Jerusalem (2 Kings 18).
Sennacherib's letter to Hezekiah again named the king of Ivvah (2 Kings 19).
Isaiah records the same boast about Ivvah, before God struck the Assyrian army (Isaiah 37).

name: Paphos
what: A city on the southwest coast of Cyprus, seat of the Roman proconsul.
today: Paphos (Kato Paphos), on the southwest coast of Cyprus
key: Barnabas and Saul traveled through Cyprus from Salamis as far as Paphos (Acts 13).
There they met the magician Bar-Jesus and the proconsul Sergius Paulus (Acts 13).
When Elymas was struck blind, the proconsul believed (Acts 13).
From Paphos Paul and his companions set sail for Perga in Pamphylia (Acts 13).

name: Persia
what: The empire that conquered Babylon and allowed the Jewish exiles to return home.
today: Iran
key: Cyrus king of Persia decreed that the exiles could rebuild the temple (2 Chronicles 36).
Opponents hired counselors to frustrate the rebuilding through the reign of Cyrus of Persia (Ezra 4).
King Ahasuerus held a great feast for the officials of Persia and Media (Esther 1).
Daniel's vision of a ram represented the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8).
An angel told Daniel the prince of Persia had withstood him (Daniel 10).

name: Media
what: The land of the Medes, northwest of Persia, later joined with Persia in one empire.
today: Northwestern Iran, around Hamadan.
key: Cyrus' decree for rebuilding the temple was found at Ecbatana in Media (Ezra 6).
Ahasuerus feasted with the army chiefs of Persia and Media (Esther 1).
Isaiah called Elam and Media to besiege Babylon (Isaiah 21).
Daniel's vision showed a two-horned ram representing the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8).

name: Ecbatana
what: The capital of Media and a summer residence of Persian kings, where royal records were kept.
today: Hamadan, in western Iran.
key: Darius searched the royal archives, and Cyrus's decree to rebuild the temple was found at Ecbatana (Ezra 6).
Darius then ordered the rebuilding to continue, with costs paid from the royal revenue (Ezra 6).

name: Aram
what: The land of the Arameans north and northeast of Israel, centered on Damascus.
today: Mainly modern Syria.
key: Balaam said Balak had brought him from Aram (Numbers 23).
David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus (2 Samuel 8).
Absalom made a vow while living at Geshur in Aram (2 Samuel 15).
Hosea recalled that Jacob fled to the land of Aram (Hosea 12).

name: Cyprus
what: A large island in the eastern Mediterranean Sea.
today: The island of Cyprus.
key: The prophets mention Cyprus as a distant coastland trading with Tyre (Ezekiel 27).
Barnabas, a Levite native of Cyprus, sold a field and gave the money to the apostles (Acts 4).
Believers scattered after Stephen's death spread the word as far as Cyprus (Acts 11).
Barnabas and Saul preached across Cyprus, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed (Acts 13).
Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus after parting with Paul (Acts 15).

name: Euphrates
what: The great river of Mesopotamia, often named as the far boundary of the promised land.
today: Euphrates River, through Turkey, Syria, and Iraq
key: The Euphrates is named as one of the four rivers of Eden (Genesis 2).
God promised Abram land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (Genesis 15).
Josiah was killed opposing Pharaoh Neco, who was marching to the Euphrates (2 Kings 23).
Jeremiah hid a linen loincloth by the Euphrates as a sign (Jeremiah 13).
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates for the kings from the east (Revelation 16).

name: Euphrates River
what: The Euphrates, often called simply the River, the great river of Mesopotamia.
today: The Euphrates River, flowing through Turkey, Syria, and Iraq.
key: Balak sent for Balaam at Pethor, near the River (Numbers 22).
God promised Israel territory reaching to the River (Deuteronomy 11).
Joshua reminded Israel that their fathers served other gods beyond the River (Joshua 24).
Isaiah warned that the Lord would use the king of Assyria from beyond the River (Isaiah 7).
Zechariah foresaw the coming king ruling from the River to the ends of the earth (Zechariah 9).

name: Hamath
what: A city-kingdom on the Orontes River in Syria, marking Israel's ideal northern border.
today: Hama, Syria
key: Toi king of Hamath sent his son to congratulate David on his victory (2 Samuel 8).
Jeroboam II restored Israel's border as far as Hamath (2 Kings 14).
People from Hamath were resettled in Samaria by the Assyrians (2 Kings 17).
Zedekiah's sons were killed before him at Riblah in the land of Hamath (2 Kings 25).

name: Lebo-hamath
what: A place in the north marking the ideal northern border of Israel's land.
today: Possibly Lebweh in the northern Beqaa Valley of Lebanon.
key: The twelve spies explored the land as far north as Lebo-hamath (Numbers 13).
God set Lebo-hamath on the northern boundary of the land (Numbers 34).
All Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt celebrated the temple's dedication (1 Kings 8).
Jeroboam II restored Israel's border from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kings 14).

name: Arpad
what: An Aramean city-state in northern Syria conquered by Assyria.
today: Tell Rifaat, north of Aleppo, Syria.
key: The Assyrian commander mocked Jerusalem by asking where the gods of Arpad were (2 Kings 18).
Sennacherib's letter to Hezekiah named the fallen king of Arpad (2 Kings 19).
God described Assyria boasting that Calno, Hamath, and Arpad had all fallen (Isaiah 10).
Jeremiah foretold that Hamath and Arpad would be confounded at bad news (Jeremiah 49).

name: Casiphia
what: A place in Babylonia where a community of Levites and temple servants lived during the exile.
today: Exact site unknown; in Babylonia, likely near Babylon, Iraq.
key: Finding no Levites among the returnees, Ezra sent men to Iddo, the leader at Casiphia (Ezra 8).
Iddo's community sent Sherebiah and other Levites, along with 220 temple servants, to join Ezra (Ezra 8).

name: Crete
what: A large island in the Mediterranean Sea south of Greece.
today: Crete, Greece.
key: Paul's ship sailed along Crete, and leaving it led to a fierce storm (Acts 27).
Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1).

name: Caphtor
what: The coastland from which the Philistines originally came, across the Mediterranean.
today: Likely the island of Crete.
key: The Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed the Avvim and settled in their place (Deuteronomy 2).
Jeremiah calls the Philistines the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor (Jeremiah 47).
God says he brought the Philistines from Caphtor, as he brought Israel from Egypt (Amos 9).

name: Malta
what: A Mediterranean island south of Sicily where Paul was shipwrecked on his voyage to Rome.
today: Malta, an island nation south of Sicily.
key: The ship carrying Paul ran aground, and all on board reached land safely (Acts 27).
The islanders showed unusual kindness, and Paul survived a viper's bite unharmed (Acts 28).
Paul healed the father of Publius, the island's chief man, and others who were sick (Acts 28).
After three months the travelers sailed on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered there (Acts 28).

name: Tigris
what: One of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia, named among the rivers flowing from Eden.
today: The Tigris River, flowing through Turkey and Iraq.
key: The Tigris is the third river from Eden, flowing east of Assyria (Genesis 2).
Standing beside the Tigris, Daniel saw a glorious man clothed in linen (Daniel 10).

name: Antioch
what: A great city of Roman Syria where believers were first called Christians.
today: Antakya, southern Turkey
key: Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch, was chosen as one of the seven (Acts 6).
Disciples in Antioch were first called Christians (Acts 11).
The church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Saul on their first mission (Acts 13).
Paul and Barnabas brought the Jerusalem council's letter to Antioch (Acts 15).
Paul opposed Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile believers (Galatians 2).

name: Habor
what: A river in upper Mesopotamia, the river of Gozan, where Assyria resettled exiled Israelites.
today: The Khabur River in northeastern Syria.
key: After Samaria fell, the king of Assyria placed Israelites by the Habor, the river of Gozan (2 Kings 17).
The account of Israel's exile to the Habor is repeated in Hezekiah's reign (2 Kings 18).
Reubenites, Gadites, and half of Manasseh were exiled to Habor and nearby places (1 Chronicles 5).

name: Halah
what: A district in Assyria where the king resettled Israelites exiled from Samaria.
today: Exact site uncertain; likely in northern Iraq, northeast of Nineveh.
key: The king of Assyria carried Israel away and placed them in Halah (2 Kings 17).
Halah is named again in the account of Samaria's fall during Hezekiah's reign (2 Kings 18).
Exiles from Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh were taken to Halah (1 Chronicles 5).

name: Assyria
what: A powerful Mesopotamian empire on the upper Tigris that conquered the northern kingdom of Israel.
today: Northern Iraq
key: The Tigris is described as flowing east of Assyria (Genesis 2).
The king of Assyria captured Samaria and deported Israel because of their sin (2 Kings 17).
Sennacherib invaded Judah, but the angel of the LORD struck his army (2 Kings 19).
God calls Assyria the rod of his anger against a godless nation (Isaiah 10).
Nahum announced the downfall of Assyria's capital, Nineveh (Nahum 3).

name: Nineveh
what: The great capital of the Assyrian Empire on the Tigris River.
today: Ruins at Mosul, northern Iraq
key: Nineveh was built in the land of Assyria (Genesis 10).
Sennacherib returned to Nineveh and was killed by his sons (2 Kings 19).
The people of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and God relented (Jonah 3).
Nahum announced the destruction of Nineveh, the bloody city (Nahum 3).
Jesus said the men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment (Matthew 12).

name: Asshur
what: The ancient heartland of Assyria and its first capital, often standing for the Assyrian nation.
today: Qal'at Sherqat, on the Tigris River in northern Iraq.
key: Balaam foretells that Asshur will take the Kenites captive and later be afflicted (Numbers 24).
The psalmist names Asshur among nations conspiring against God's people (Psalms 83).
Merchants of Asshur trade fine garments with Tyre (Ezekiel 27).

name: Immer
what: A settlement in Babylonia from which some exiles returned who could not prove their Israelite descent.
today: Exact site unknown; in Babylonia, Iraq.
key: Returnees from Immer and nearby places could not prove their families belonged to Israel (Ezra 2).
Nehemiah's copy of the list records the same returnees from Immer (Nehemiah 7).

name: Pethor
what: Balaam's hometown near the Euphrates River in upper Mesopotamia.
today: Likely ancient Pitru, near Carchemish in northern Syria.
key: King Balak of Moab sent messengers to Balaam at Pethor to curse Israel (Numbers 22).
Moses recalls that Balaam son of Beor was hired from Pethor to curse Israel (Deuteronomy 23).

name: Carchemish
what: A major city on the upper Euphrates, site of a decisive battle between Egypt and Babylon.
today: Ruins at Karkamis on the Turkey–Syria border, near Jarabulus.
key: King Josiah was killed opposing Pharaoh Neco on his way to fight at Carchemish (2 Chronicles 35).
Assyria boasts that conquered cities, including Carchemish, show its power is unstoppable (Isaiah 10).
Nebuchadnezzar defeated Neco's army at Carchemish by the Euphrates (Jeremiah 46).

name: Gozan
what: A region on the Habor River in upper Mesopotamia, where Assyria resettled exiled Israelites.
today: Tell Halaf area, in northeastern Syria.
key: Assyria exiled Israelites to the Habor, the river of Gozan (2 Kings 17).
Sennacherib boasted that the gods of Gozan had not saved it (2 Kings 19).
Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh were taken to Gozan (1 Chronicles 5).

name: Haran
what: A city in upper Mesopotamia where Abraham's family settled and Laban lived.
today: Harran, in southeastern Turkey near the Syrian border.
key: Terah settled in Haran with Abram and died there (Genesis 11).
Abram left Haran for Canaan at the Lord's call, aged seventy-five (Genesis 12).
Rebekah sent Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran to escape Esau (Genesis 27).
Jacob met Rachel by a well near Haran (Genesis 29).
Sennacherib boasted that Assyria had destroyed Haran (2 Kings 19).

name: Paddan-aram
what: The region of upper Mesopotamia around Haran, home of Abraham's relatives.
today: The area around Harran in southeastern Turkey and northern Syria.
key: Isaac married Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram (Genesis 25).
Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan-aram to take a wife from Laban's daughters (Genesis 28).
Jacob left Paddan-aram with the livestock he had gained there (Genesis 31).
God appeared to Jacob again after he came from Paddan-aram and renamed him Israel (Genesis 35).

name: Cilicia
what: A region in southeastern Asia Minor whose chief city was Tarsus, Paul's birthplace.
today: The southern coastal region of Turkey around Tarsus and Adana.
key: Men from Cilicia disputed with Stephen (Acts 6).
The Jerusalem council sent its letter to Gentile believers in Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15).
Paul identified himself as a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21).
Paul sailed past Cilicia on his voyage toward Rome (Acts 27).
After his conversion, Paul went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1).

name: Tarsus
what: A major city of Cilicia in Asia Minor and the birthplace of the apostle Paul.
today: Tarsus, in south-central Turkey.
key: The Lord tells Ananias to seek a man of Tarsus named Saul (Acts 9).
Believers send Saul away to Tarsus after Jews in Jerusalem seek to kill him (Acts 9).
Barnabas goes to Tarsus to find Saul and brings him to Antioch (Acts 11).
Paul tells the Roman tribune he is a citizen of Tarsus, no obscure city (Acts 21).
Paul tells the Jerusalem crowd he was born in Tarsus but raised in Jerusalem (Acts 22).

name: Tarshish
what: A distant trading port, probably in the western Mediterranean, known for its large seagoing ships.
today: Possibly Tartessus in southern Spain; exact site unknown
key: Solomon's fleet of Tarshish ships brought gold, silver, and ivory every three years (1 Kings 10).
Jehoshaphat's ships built to sail to Tarshish were wrecked (2 Chronicles 20).
The psalmist prays that the kings of Tarshish will bring tribute (Psalms 72).
Jonah boarded a ship bound for Tarshish to flee from the LORD (Jonah 1).

name: Luz
what: A city built in the land of the Hittites by a man spared when Joseph's tribes captured Bethel.
today: Exact site unknown; in the land of the Hittites, north of Israel.
key: A man of Luz showed Joseph's spies the way into the city, and he and his family were spared (Judges 1).
He went to the land of the Hittites, built a city, and named it Luz (Judges 1).

name: Pamphylia
what: A coastal region of southern Asia Minor, with Perga as a main city.
today: The Antalya region of southern Turkey.
key: Visitors from Pamphylia heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2).
John Mark left Paul and Barnabas at Perga in Pamphylia (Acts 13).
Paul and Barnabas passed through Pamphylia on their return (Acts 14).
Paul refused to take Mark because he had withdrawn in Pamphylia (Acts 15).
Paul's ship sailed past Cilicia and Pamphylia toward Rome (Acts 27).

name: Perga
what: A city in Pamphylia on the southern coast of Asia Minor, visited on Paul's first journey.
today: Ruins near Aksu, east of Antalya in southern Turkey.
key: At Perga, John Mark left Paul and Barnabas and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13).
On their return, Paul and Barnabas spoke the word in Perga before sailing home (Acts 14).

name: Patmos
what: A small rocky island in the Aegean Sea where John received the book of Revelation.
today: Patmos, a Greek island in the Dodecanese, Aegean Sea.
key: John was on Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (Revelation 1).
In the Spirit on the Lord's day, John was told to write to seven churches (Revelation 1).
John saw the glorified Christ standing among seven golden lampstands (Revelation 1).

name: Derbe
what: A city of Lycaonia in Asia Minor where Paul preached on his missionary journeys.
today: Likely Kerti Huyuk, near Karaman, south-central Turkey.
key: Paul and Barnabas preach in Derbe and make many disciples after Paul is stoned (Acts 14).
Paul returns to Derbe and Lystra, where he meets Timothy (Acts 16).
Gaius of Derbe travels with Paul toward Jerusalem (Acts 20).

name: Miletus
what: A port city on the western coast of Asia Minor, south of Ephesus.
today: Ruins near the village of Balat in western Turkey.
key: Paul sent for the Ephesian elders to meet him at Miletus and gave them a farewell charge (Acts 20).
Paul tells Timothy he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4).

name: Galatia
what: A Roman province in central Asia Minor where Paul planted churches.
today: Central Turkey, around Ankara and Konya.
key: Paul and Silas traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia (Acts 16).
Paul went through Galatia again, strengthening the disciples (Acts 18).
Paul directed the churches of Galatia about the collection for the saints (1 Corinthians 16).
Paul wrote his letter to the churches of Galatia (Galatians 1).
Peter addressed his first letter to believers scattered in Galatia and nearby provinces (1 Peter 1).

name: Lystra
what: A Roman colony in Lycaonia in south-central Asia Minor, hometown of Timothy.
today: Ruins near Hatunsaray, south of Konya, Turkey.
key: Paul healed a lame man at Lystra, and the crowds hailed him and Barnabas as gods (Acts 14).
Paul was stoned at Lystra and left for dead, but rose and went on (Acts 14).
Paul met Timothy at Lystra and took him along (Acts 16).
Paul reminded Timothy of the persecutions he endured at Lystra (2 Timothy 3).

name: Laodicea
what: A prosperous city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor, near Colossae and Hierapolis.
today: Ruins near Denizli, in southwestern Turkey.
key: Paul told the Colossians he was struggling for those at Laodicea (Colossians 2).
Paul asked that his letters be exchanged between Colossae and Laodicea (Colossians 4).
Laodicea was one of the seven churches to receive John's message (Revelation 1).
Jesus rebuked the Laodicean church as lukewarm and called it to repent (Revelation 3).

name: Phrygia
what: A region in the interior of Asia Minor, west of Galatia.
today: West-central Turkey.
key: Jews from Phrygia were among those who heard the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2).
Paul and his companions went through Phrygia and Galatia, kept from preaching in Asia (Acts 16).
Paul traveled through Phrygia strengthening all the disciples (Acts 18).

name: Colossae
what: A city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor, home of the church to which Paul wrote Colossians.
today: Unexcavated mound near Honaz, Denizli Province, southwestern Turkey
key: Paul and Timothy wrote to the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae (Colossians 1).
The Colossians had learned the gospel from Epaphras, Paul's beloved fellow servant (Colossians 1).
Paul sent Tychicus with Onesimus, one of their own, to tell them his news (Colossians 4).
He asked that the letter also be read in the church of the Laodiceans (Colossians 4).

name: Iconium
what: A city in south-central Asia Minor visited by Paul on his missionary journeys.
today: Konya, in central Turkey.
key: Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet at Antioch and went to Iconium (Acts 13).
Many believed at Iconium, but a plot to stone the apostles forced them to flee (Acts 14).
The believers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of Timothy (Acts 16).
Paul reminded Timothy of the persecutions he endured at Iconium (2 Timothy 3).

name: Lycaonia
what: A region of south-central Asia Minor containing the cities of Lystra and Derbe.
today: The Konya plain in south-central Turkey.
key: Driven from Iconium, Paul and Barnabas fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia (Acts 14).
After Paul healed a lame man, the crowd shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down (Acts 14).
The people called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes and tried to offer sacrifices to them (Acts 14).

name: Corinth
what: A wealthy Greek port city and capital of the Roman province of Achaia.
today: Ruins near modern Corinth, Greece.
key: Paul stayed in Corinth a year and a half with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18).
Apollos ministered at Corinth while Paul was in Ephesus (Acts 19).
Paul wrote to the church of God in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1).
Paul explained he had spared the Corinthians by not returning yet (2 Corinthians 1).
Erastus remained at Corinth (2 Timothy 4).

name: Hierapolis
what: A city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Colossae.
today: Pamukkale, near Denizli, Turkey.
key: Epaphras of Colossae worked hard in prayer for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 4).
Paul names Hierapolis with Laodicea and Colossae, neighboring cities where believers gathered (Colossians 4).

name: Ephesus
what: A major port city in the Roman province of Asia where Paul ministered for over two years.
today: Ruins near Selçuk, western Turkey
key: Paul left Priscilla and Aquila at Ephesus (Acts 18).
A riot broke out in Ephesus over the goddess Artemis (Acts 19).
Paul said farewell to the elders of the church at Ephesus (Acts 20).
Paul urged Timothy to remain at Ephesus and correct false teachers (1 Timothy 1).
Christ told the church in Ephesus it had abandoned its first love (Revelation 2).

name: Javan
what: The Hebrew name for the Greek peoples, especially the Ionians of western Asia Minor and the Aegean.
today: Greece and the western coast of Turkey.
key: Javan is listed as a son of Japheth, ancestor of the coastland peoples (Genesis 10).
Javan is named among distant nations who will hear of the Lord's glory (Isaiah 66).
Javan traded slaves and bronze vessels with the city of Tyre (Ezekiel 27).
In Daniel's vision, the shaggy goat represents the king of Greece (Daniel 8).

name: Achaia
what: The Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.
today: Southern Greece, including Corinth and Athens.
key: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, dismissed the Jews' charges against Paul in Corinth (Acts 18).
Paul resolved to pass through Macedonia and Achaia before going to Jerusalem (Acts 19).
Believers in Achaia gave a contribution for the poor saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15).
Stephanas' household were the first converts in Achaia (1 Corinthians 16).
The faith of the Thessalonians became an example to believers in Achaia (1 Thessalonians 1).

name: Athens
what: The leading city of ancient Greece, famed for its philosophy and temples.
today: Athens, Greece.
key: Paul preached at the Areopagus in Athens, and some believed (Acts 17).
Paul left Athens and went to Corinth (Acts 18).
Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3).

name: Greece
what: The land of the Greeks, which became a world empire under Alexander the Great.
today: Greece.
key: Daniel's vision of a goat represented the king of Greece (Daniel 8).
An angel spoke of the coming prince of Greece (Daniel 10).
A Persian king would stir up all against the kingdom of Greece (Daniel 11).
God promised to rouse Zion's sons against the sons of Greece (Zechariah 9).
Paul spent three months in Greece (Acts 20).

name: Areopagus
what: A rocky hill in Athens and the name of the council that met there.
today: A hill northwest of the Acropolis in Athens, Greece.
key: Athenian philosophers bring Paul to the Areopagus to hear his new teaching (Acts 17).
Paul proclaims the unknown god as the Creator who raised Jesus from the dead (Acts 17).
Dionysius the Areopagite and others believe (Acts 17).

name: Pisidian Antioch
what: A Roman colony in the region of Pisidia in Asia Minor, visited by Paul on his first missionary journey.
today: Ruins near Yalvac, in west-central Turkey.
key: Paul preaches in the synagogue, and many Gentiles believe, but Jews drive him out (Acts 13).
Jews from Antioch stir up crowds in Lystra, who stone Paul (Acts 14).
Paul and Barnabas return to strengthen the disciples in Antioch (Acts 14).
Paul reminds Timothy of the persecutions he endured at Antioch (2 Timothy 3).

name: Pisidia
what: A mountainous region of southern Asia Minor visited by Paul on his first missionary journey.
today: The Taurus Mountains region of south-central Turkey.
key: Paul and Barnabas came to Antioch in Pisidia, and Paul preached in the synagogue (Acts 13).
Returning from Lystra and Iconium, they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia (Acts 14).

name: Philadelphia
what: A city in the Roman province of Asia, home of one of the seven churches of Revelation.
today: Alaşehir, western Turkey.
key: Philadelphia is one of seven churches John is told to write to (Revelation 1).
Christ says the church has kept his word and gives it an open door (Revelation 3).
He promises to keep them from the hour of trial coming on the world (Revelation 3).
The one who conquers will be made a pillar in the temple of God (Revelation 3).

name: Smyrna
what: A port city of the Roman province of Asia, home of one of the seven churches of Revelation.
today: İzmir, western Turkey.
key: Smyrna is one of seven churches John is told to write to (Revelation 1).
Christ knows the church's tribulation and poverty, yet says it is rich (Revelation 2).
He tells them to be faithful unto death and promises the crown of life (Revelation 2).

name: Sardis
what: A wealthy city in western Asia Minor, home to one of the seven churches of Revelation.
today: Ruins near Sart, east of Izmir in western Turkey.
key: Sardis is one of seven cities whose churches John is told to write to (Revelation 1).
Christ tells Sardis it has a reputation for being alive but is dead (Revelation 3).
A few in Sardis have not soiled their garments and will walk with Christ in white (Revelation 3).

name: Thyatira
what: A trading city in the Roman province of Asia, home of one of the seven churches of Revelation.
today: Akhisar, in western Turkey.
key: Lydia, a seller of purple goods from Thyatira, believes Paul's message in Philippi (Acts 16).
Thyatira is named among the seven churches receiving John's book (Revelation 1).
Jesus commends Thyatira's love and service but rebukes its tolerance of Jezebel (Revelation 2).

name: Nicopolis
what: A city where Paul decided to spend the winter, asking Titus to join him there.
today: Likely Nicopolis in Epirus, near Preveza, western Greece
key: Paul told Titus to come to him at Nicopolis once Artemas or Tychicus arrived (Titus 3).
Paul had decided to spend the winter there (Titus 3).

name: Pergamum
what: A leading city of the Roman province of Asia, home of one of the seven churches of Revelation.
today: Ruins beside Bergama, western Turkey.
key: Pergamum is one of seven churches John is told to write to (Revelation 1).
Christ says the church lives where Satan's throne is, yet held fast when Antipas was killed (Revelation 2).
He rebukes some there for holding the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans (Revelation 2).
He promises the one who conquers hidden manna and a white stone (Revelation 2).

name: Asia
what: The Roman province in western Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its leading city.
today: Western Turkey
key: People from Asia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2).
The Holy Spirit kept Paul from speaking the word in Asia at first (Acts 16).
During Paul's two years in Ephesus, all the residents of Asia heard the word (Acts 19).
Paul reminded the Ephesian elders how he had lived among them in Asia (Acts 20).
John wrote to the seven churches in Asia (Revelation 1).

name: Troas
what: A Roman port city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, near ancient Troy.
today: Ruins of Alexandria Troas, in northwestern Turkey.
key: At Troas Paul saw a vision of a man of Macedonia calling for help (Acts 16).
Paul raised Eutychus after he fell from a window at Troas (Acts 20).
A door opened for the gospel at Troas, but Paul left without finding Titus (2 Corinthians 2).
Paul had left his cloak with Carpus at Troas (2 Timothy 4).

name: Ararat
what: A mountainous land north of Assyria where Noah's ark came to rest after the flood.
today: Eastern Turkey and Armenia, the region of the ancient kingdom of Urartu.
key: As the flood waters receded, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat (Genesis 8).
After killing their father Sennacherib, his sons escaped to the land of Ararat (2 Kings 19).
Jeremiah summoned the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz against Babylon (Jeremiah 51).

name: Beth-togarmah
what: A people and land of the far north, named for Togarmah and known for trading horses and mules.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly eastern Turkey or Armenia.
key: Beth-togarmah traded horses, war horses, and mules for the wares of Tyre (Ezekiel 27).
Beth-togarmah from the uttermost parts of the north is named among the allies of Gog (Ezekiel 38).

name: Spain
what: The Roman lands of the Iberian Peninsula at the western end of the Mediterranean.
today: Spain and Portugal, on the Iberian Peninsula.
key: Paul hoped to visit the Roman believers on his way to Spain (Romans 15).
After delivering the gift to Jerusalem, Paul planned to go by way of Rome to Spain (Romans 15).

name: Berea
what: A city in Macedonia where the Jews eagerly examined the Scriptures after hearing Paul preach.
today: Veria, in northern Greece.
key: After the riot in Thessalonica, believers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea (Acts 17).
The Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to check Paul's teaching, and many believed (Acts 17).
Jews from Thessalonica stirred up the crowds, so Paul left while Silas and Timothy remained (Acts 17).
Sopater of Berea traveled with Paul toward Jerusalem (Acts 20).

name: Minni
what: A kingdom in the mountains north of Assyria, summoned with Ararat and Ashkenaz against Babylon.
today: Likely the region south of Lake Urmia, northwestern Iran.
key: Jeremiah summoned the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz to war against Babylon (Jeremiah 51).
They were called up with the kings of the Medes as instruments of the LORD's judgment (Jeremiah 51).

name: Macedonia
what: The Roman province in northern Greece, including Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea.
today: Northern Greece and North Macedonia
key: Paul saw a vision of a man of Macedonia pleading for help (Acts 16).
Paul passed through Macedonia encouraging the churches (Acts 20).
The churches of Macedonia gave generously despite deep poverty (2 Corinthians 8).
The Philippians supported Paul when he left Macedonia (Philippians 4).
The word of the Lord sounded forth from the Thessalonians in Macedonia (1 Thessalonians 1).

name: Thessalonica
what: The chief city of the Roman province of Macedonia, on the Aegean coast.
today: Thessaloniki, Greece.
key: Paul preached three Sabbaths in Thessalonica before a mob forced him out (Acts 17).
Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, sailed with Paul to Rome (Acts 27).
The Philippians sent help to Paul more than once in Thessalonica (Philippians 4).
Demas deserted Paul and went to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4).

name: Tubal
what: A distant nation descended from Japheth, often paired with Meshech, known for trading slaves and bronze.
today: Likely central or eastern Anatolia, in modern Turkey.
key: God will send survivors to distant nations, including Tubal, to declare his glory (Isaiah 66).
Tubal traded slaves and bronze vessels with the merchants of Tyre (Ezekiel 27).
Gog is called chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and God declares himself against him (Ezekiel 38).
God promises to defeat Gog, prince of Meshech and Tubal, on the mountains of Israel (Ezekiel 39).

name: Pontus
what: A region of northern Asia Minor along the southern shore of the Black Sea.
today: The Black Sea coast of northern Turkey.
key: Jews from Pontus were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2).
Paul met Aquila, a Jew native to Pontus, in Corinth (Acts 18).
Peter addressed his first letter to God's scattered people in Pontus and nearby regions (1 Peter 1).

name: Philippi
what: A leading Roman colony in Macedonia and the first place in Europe where Paul planted a church.
today: Ruins near Krinides, northeastern Greece.
key: Lydia believes, a slave girl is freed, and a jailer is converted (Acts 16).
Paul sails from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread (Acts 20).
Paul writes to the saints at Philippi with their overseers and deacons (Philippians 1).
Paul recalls being shamefully treated at Philippi before coming to Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 2).

name: Rome
what: The capital city of the Roman Empire.
today: Rome, the capital of Italy.
key: Visitors from Rome heard the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2).
Aquila and Priscilla had left Rome when Claudius expelled the Jews (Acts 18).
The Lord told Paul he must testify about him in Rome (Acts 23).
Paul lived in Rome under guard for two years, proclaiming the kingdom of God (Acts 28).
Paul wrote to all God's beloved in Rome, eager to preach the gospel there (Romans 1).

name: Italy
what: The Roman peninsula, home of the imperial capital Rome.
today: Italy.
key: Aquila and Priscilla have recently come from Italy after Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome (Acts 18).
Paul sails for Italy as a prisoner under the centurion Julius (Acts 27).
Those from Italy send greetings to the letter's readers (Hebrews 13).

name: Meshech
what: A distant northern people and land, often named with Tubal.
today: Likely in central or eastern Turkey.
key: The psalmist laments living as a sojourner in Meshech (Psalms 120).
Meshech traded slaves and bronze with Tyre (Ezekiel 27).
Ezekiel prophesied against Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal (Ezekiel 38).
God declared he would turn Gog of Meshech back and defeat him (Ezekiel 39).

name: Magog
what: A distant northern land, home of Gog, who leads the nations against God's people.
today: Exact site unknown; a remote northern region, possibly in Asia Minor.
key: Ezekiel prophesies against Gog of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal (Ezekiel 38).
God promises to send fire on Magog and make his holy name known (Ezekiel 39).
After the thousand years, Satan gathers Gog and Magog for a final battle (Revelation 20).
